meta.title: Who really said "Play it again, Sam"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Nobody. In Casablanca (1942) Ilsa says "Play it, Sam. Play 'As Time Goes By.'" and Rick says "Play it!" The famous wording is in no scene of the film.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Play it again, Sam'?
meta.ogDescription: Nobody says it in Casablanca. Ilsa says "Play it, Sam. Play 'As Time Goes By.'" Bogart never says the famous line at all. What the script really has.

answer.label: Not quite — the actual line is “Play it, Sam. Play ‘As Time Goes By.’”
answer.authorName: Julius J. Epstein, Philip G. Epstein & Howard Koch
answer.authorDates: Credited screenwriters of Casablanca (1942), adapting Burnett & Alison’s 1940 play
answer.sourceLine: Nobody says “Play it again, Sam” in Casablanca. Ilsa Lund says “Play it once, Sam, for old times’ sake,” then “Play it, Sam. Play ‘As Time Goes By.’” Rick’s version, later, is “You played it for her, you can play it for me … Play it!” The popular wording fuses her request with his insistence and adds a word that appears in neither.
answer.confidenceText: The wording is wrong, not the film: the line “Play it again, Sam” is in no scene of the picture.

source.heading: What the script actually says

docMeta.dd: Julius J. Epstein, Philip G. Epstein & Howard Koch — a shared credit; no one of the three can be singled out for this line
Ilsa Lund (Ingrid Bergman) — a fictional character, not the author
Everybody Comes to Rick’s (1940), an unproduced play by Murray Burnett & Joan Alison

source.excerpt:
ILSA: Play it once, Sam, for old times’ sake.
SAM: I don’t know what you mean, Miss Ilsa.
ILSA: [whispers] Play it, Sam. Play “As Time Goes By.”
SAM: Why, I can’t remember it, Miss Ilsa. I’m a little rusty on it.
ILSA: I’ll hum it for you.
trail: The film itself settles it. Wikiquote’s Misattributed section ↗ states that while the lines “Play it” and “Play it, Sam” both appear in the film, the line “Play it again, Sam” never appears in the film. Quote Investigator has no entry on this phrase, so Wikiquote’s sourced transcription is the anchor here.

The real line is honoured under its real wording. The American Film Institute ranked “Play it, Sam. Play ‘As Time Goes By.’” at No. 28 ↗ of its 100 greatest movie quotations, crediting it to Ilsa Lund (Ingrid Bergman) — not to Rick, and not to Bogart.
Bogart’s nearest line is a different one. Oxford University Press, writing on the misquotation, gives Rick’s words as “If she can stand it, I can. Play it!” ↗ — the same demand, no “again,” no “Sam.”

The scene predates the screenplay; the name does not. The 1940 play Everybody Comes to Rick’s ↗ supplied both the song and the character, but its piano player is called ‘The Rabbit,’ renamed Sam for the film — so “Play it, Sam” as a form of words could not have existed on the page Burnett and Alison wrote.
source.cutTag: Casablanca (1942) · Ilsa & Sam at the piano
source.excerptNote: Transcribed dialogue per Wikiquote ↗. Note that the word “again” never occurs, and that the request is Ilsa’s. Rick’s separate, later demand runs “You played it for her, you can play it for me!…Play it!”

source.rightsNote: Casablanca premiered in 1942 and was produced and distributed by Warner Bros., well after the 1930 cutoff for the US public domain, so the screenplay remains in copyright. Screen writing is work-for-hire: the rights sit with the studio, not with the Epsteins or Howard Koch. The song “As Time Goes By” (Herman Hupfeld, 1931) is a separate copyright again, and no lyrics are reproduced here.

author.name: Julius J. Epstein, Philip G. Epstein & Howard Koch
author.heading: About Julius J. Epstein, Philip G. Epstein & Howard Koch
author.bio: The screenplay of Casablanca carries three credited writers — twin brothers Julius J. Epstein and Philip G. Epstein, who shaped the structure and the film’s celebrated wisecracks, and Howard Koch, who handled the politics. They were adapting an unproduced 1940 stage play, Everybody Comes to Rick’s, by Murray Burnett and Joan Alison. Because the credit is genuinely shared and the picture was rewritten during shooting, no single one of the three can be named as the author of this particular line — and the character Ilsa and the actress Ingrid Bergman are not its authors at all.

copyAttribution: Ilsa Lund in Casablanca (1942), screenplay by Julius J. Epstein, Philip G. Epstein and Howard Koch — "Play it, Sam. Play 'As Time Goes By.'" Commonly misquoted as "Play it again, Sam," a line that appears nowhere in the film.

misattribution.heading: Three things people get wrong about this line
misattribution.intro: This is not a case of a stolen quotation — the film is the right film. But almost every element around the sentence is off: the words, the speaker, and how much of it Casablanca invented.

items.why: The sentence appears in no scene. Wikiquote’s Misattributed section ↗ puts it flatly: while the lines “Play it” and “Play it, Sam” both appear in the film, the line “Play it again, Sam” never appears in the film.

The line closest to the misquote is Ilsa Lund’s, not Rick’s — the AFI credits “Play it, Sam. Play ‘As Time Goes By.’” to Ilsa Lund, played by Ingrid Bergman ↗. Bogart’s nearest equivalent is a different, angrier line: “You played it for her, you can play it for me!…Play it!” ↗. And an actor is never the author of a line in any case.

The moment is older than the movie. Ilsa’s request and the song both come from the 1940 stage play Everybody Comes to Rick’s — Wikipedia notes the inclusion of ‘As Time Goes By’ came from Burnett and Alison’s play ↗. What the film added is the name: in the play the piano player is not Sam but ‘The Rabbit.’ So the two most quoted words of the real line are the screenwriters’ own.

misattribution.truthLine: The real line is Ilsa’s, and it is shorter than you remember: “Play it, Sam. Play ‘As Time Goes By.’” ↗

context.heading: Why the memory beat the movie
lead: The misquote is more efficient than the real thing. Ilsa’s request is spread across a hesitant exchange — she asks once for old times’ sake, Sam plays dumb, she names the song, he claims he’s rusty, she offers to hum it. Rick’s later demand is a separate scene and a different mood: bitter rather than tender. “Play it again, Sam” compresses all of it into four words and hands them to Bogart, who never said them.

The word again is the tell. It does real work that the script deliberately leaves implied: it announces that the song has a history, that this is a repetition. The film conveys the same thing through Sam’s reluctance and Ilsa’s whisper. Popular memory, having no whisper to work with, wrote the subtext into the text.
context.detailsSummary: What the film actually gives you, in order
detailsBody: Ilsa to Sam: “Play it once, Sam, for old times’ sake.” — then, after he stalls, “Play it, Sam. Play ‘As Time Goes By.’” This is the line the American Film Institute ranked among the great movie quotations.

Rick to Sam, later and angrier: “You played it for her, you can play it for me … If she can stand it, I can. Play it!” This is the closest Bogart comes, and it still contains no “again” and no “Sam” in the imperative.
Neither speech is the popular sentence. The popular sentence is a composite that exists only outside the picture.
context.pull: The word “again” is the subtext of the scene, promoted to dialogue.
